title: CSC3710 2026-11-24: DFA Minimization and Nondeterministic Pushdown Automata

questions.q: Two DFA states p and q are distinguishable when:
choices: Some input string takes exactly one of them to a final state
Some input string takes both of them to a final state
They have different arrows on at least one input symbol
One is reachable from the start state and the other is not
questions.explain: p and q are distinguishable if some string w makes exactly one of δ*(p,w) and δ*(q,w) final. Different arrows alone don't prove anything, because the targets might behave the same way.

questions.q: A final state and a non-final state can be combined in the minimized DFA if their outgoing arrows go to the same states.
questions.explain: The empty string separates them: one accepts it and the other doesn't. Final states only combine with final states, and non-final states only with non-final states.

questions.q: Which string always distinguishes a final state from a non-final state?
choices: The empty string λ
Any string of length 1
The string a
None; the pair needs further checking
questions.explain: Reading nothing leaves each state where it is, so λ ends in a final state from one of them and a non-final state from the other. That is why step 1 marks every final/non-final pair right away.

questions.q: "p and q are distinguishable by a" means exactly one of δ(p, a) and δ(q, a) is a final state.
questions.explain: The one-symbol string a already separates them, so you can mark the pair without checking anything else.

questions.q: In a DFA over {a, b}, two non-final states q_i and q_j both go to q7 on a and both go to q2 on b. What can you conclude?
choices: They are indistinguishable and can be combined
They are distinguishable by a
They are distinguishable by b
Nothing until the auxiliary table is complete
questions.explain: If both states go to the same state on every symbol and have the same final status, then every string leads them to the same place. The pair stays 0 for sure, like (q3, q5) in the 7-state example.

questions.q: Two indistinguishable states accept exactly the same set of continuations, i.e. the same strings read from that state onward.
questions.explain: In the professor's words, from either state "I see the same landscape". That is why they can be merged into one state.

questions.q: A finished table shows (q0, q1) = 0 and (q1, q2) = 0 but (q0, q2) = 1. The table must contain an error.
questions.explain: Indistinguishability is an equivalence relation. If q0 ≡ q1 and q1 ≡ q2, then q0 ≡ q2, so (q0, q2) would also have to be 0.

questions.q: While checking pair (q1, q3), you find that on input a the target pair is (q1, q3) itself. What do you do?
choices: Drop it and try the next symbol
Mark (q1, q3) with 1
Leave (q1, q3) at 0 for good
Put (q1, q3) on its own auxiliary list
questions.explain: "1 and 3 are distinguishable if 1 and 3 are distinguishable" is circular, so this symbol is a dead end. Move on to the next symbol.

questions.q: While checking pair (q2, q4), you find that on input b both states go to q5. What does this target tell you?
choices: Drop it: q5 cannot be told apart from q5
Mark (q2, q4) with 1 because q5 is final
Put (q2, q4) on the auxiliary list of (q5, q5)
Leave (q2, q4) at 0 without checking a
questions.explain: When the target is the same state twice, that symbol cannot separate the pair. Drop it and check the remaining symbols.

questions.q: While checking pair (q0, q1), you find that on input b the target pair (q2, q3) is still 0 and undecided. What do you do?
choices: Write (q0, q1) on the auxiliary list of (q2, q3)
Write (q2, q3) on the auxiliary list of (q0, q1)
Mark (q0, q1) with 1
Leave (q0, q1) at 0 permanently
questions.explain: The entry on (q2, q3)'s list reads: "if (q2, q3) is ever marked, mark (q0, q1) too." The pair you are checking goes on the target's list, not the other way around.

questions.q: Pair (q2, q3) has just been marked 1, and its auxiliary list contains (q0, q1). What happens next?
choices: Mark (q0, q1) with 1, then anything on its list
Remove (q0, q1) from the list; it stays 0
Move (q2, q3) onto the list of (q0, q1)
Nothing until the whole table has been scanned
questions.explain: Marking a pair marks everything on its list, then everything on those pairs' lists, and so on. This chain is what lets the algorithm handle any number of states.

questions.q: The order in which you check the pairs changes which states end up combined.
questions.explain: The order doesn't matter: the result is the same. Going systematically (01, 02, 03, ..., 34) just keeps you from getting lost.

questions.q: You finish the table-filling algorithm and no cell is 0. What does that mean?
choices: The DFA is already minimal and cannot be reduced
Every pair of states can be combined
The algorithm must be run a second time
The DFA accepts no strings at all
questions.explain: A 1 means distinguishable. If every pair is distinguishable, there is nothing to merge, so the DFA cannot be minimized.

questions.q: At the end of the algorithm, cell (q1, q3) still holds 0. What does it mean?
choices: q1 and q3 are indistinguishable and can be merged
q1 and q3 are distinguishable by every string
The check of (q1, q3) was never finished
q1 and q3 must both be non-final trap states
questions.explain: Any 0 left at the end is permanent ("nothing can help it"), and each 0 is a pair of states you can combine.

questions.q: A DFA has 6 states, and exactly one of them is final. After step 1 (marking every final/non-final pair), how many pairs are left to check?
questions.explain: There are C(6,2) = 15 pairs. The final state pairs with each of the 5 non-final states, so 5 pairs are marked in step 1, which leaves 10.

questions.q: A DFA has 7 states, and exactly one of them is non-final. After step 1 (marking every final/non-final pair), how many pairs are left to check?
questions.explain: There are C(7,2) = 21 pairs. The non-final state pairs with each of the 6 final states, so 6 pairs are marked in step 1, which leaves 15.

questions.q: In the "distinguishable by a or by b" pre-pass, what do you do with a pair that is distinguishable by a?
choices: Mark it 1 and move on without checking b
Check b as well before marking it
Put it on the auxiliary list of its a-targets
Leave it for the main pass as a hard case
questions.explain: One distinguishing symbol is enough. You only look at b when a fails to separate the pair.

questions.q: Why does the pre-pass make the rest of the table-filling algorithm easier?
choices: Hard cases then often hit an already-marked pair
It finds every indistinguishable pair directly
It removes the need for step 1 (final vs non-final)
It changes which states end up combined
questions.explain: Each extra 1 gives the hard cases a marked target to point at, so most of them are settled in one look and the auxiliary table is rarely needed. The final result does not change.

questions.q: If a pair is distinguishable neither by a nor by b in the pre-pass, it must be indistinguishable.
questions.explain: It is only a hard case: its answer depends on other pairs, and a longer string may still separate the states. For example, in the 6-state example (q0, q1) is separated by bb.

questions.q: DFA B over {a, b}: start state q0; every state is final except q6. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q2; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q1, b→q3; q3: a→q4, b→q6; q4: a→q4, b→q5; q5: a→q4, b→q6; q6: a→q6, b→q6. After the pre-pass you check (q0, q2): on a both go to q1, and on b the target is (q2, q3). What is the decision?
choices: Mark (q0, q2) with 1, since (q2, q3) is already marked
Leave (q0, q2) at 0 forever
Put (q0, q2) on the auxiliary list of (q2, q3)
Put (q2, q3) on the auxiliary list of (q0, q2)
questions.explain: (q2, q3) is distinguishable by b (q3 goes to the non-final q6, q2 goes to the final q3), so the pre-pass already marked it. Thanks to that, no auxiliary list is needed.

questions.q: DFA A over {a, b}: start state q0, only final state q5. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q3; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q2, b→q5; q3: a→q3, b→q4; q4: a→q4, b→q5. Select every pair that is distinguishable by b.
questions.explain: On b, q2 and q4 go to the final state q5, while q0, q1 and q3 go to non-final states. A pair is distinguishable by b exactly when it has one state from each group. (q2, q4) both reach q5, and (q0, q1) and (q1, q3) both reach non-final states.

questions.q: DFA A over {a, b}: start state q0, only final state q5. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q3; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q2, b→q5; q3: a→q3, b→q4; q4: a→q4, b→q5. Which states end up combined?
choices: {q1, q3} and {q2, q4}
{q1, q2} and {q3, q4}
{q0, q1} and {q2, q3}
{q0, q1, q3} and {q2, q4}
questions.explain: Only (q1, q3) and (q2, q4) stay 0. q0 is separated from q1 by bb (q1 reaches q5, q0 reaches q4), and from q3 by bb as well.

questions.q: DFA A over {a, b}: start state q0, only final state q5. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q3; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q2, b→q5; q3: a→q3, b→q4; q4: a→q4, b→q5. How many states does the minimized DFA have?
questions.explain: The classes are {q0}, {q1, q3}, {q2, q4} and {q5}, so the DFA goes from 6 states to 4.

questions.q: DFA A over {a, b}: start state q0, only final state q5. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q3; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q2, b→q5; q3: a→q3, b→q4; q4: a→q4, b→q5. Why does pair (q2, q4) stay 0 no matter what?
choices: On a it maps to itself; on b both go to q5
Both q2 and q4 are final states
Neither state can ever reach a final state
It was never put on any auxiliary list
questions.explain: On a the target is (q2, q4) again, which is circular. On b both states go to q5, the same state. Neither symbol can ever lead to a marked pair.

questions.q: DFA A over {a, b}: start state q0, only final state q5. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q3; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q2, b→q5; q3: a→q3, b→q4; q4: a→q4, b→q5. Pair (q1, q3) stays 0 because the pair it waits on, (q2, q4), is never marked.
questions.explain: On a, (q1, q3) maps to itself, so that is a dead end. On b it goes to (q2, q4), so (q1, q3) sits on (q2, q4)'s list. (q2, q4) stays 0, so (q1, q3) is never marked.

questions.q: DFA B over {a, b}: start state q0; every state is final except q6. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q2; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q1, b→q3; q3: a→q4, b→q6; q4: a→q4, b→q5; q5: a→q4, b→q6; q6: a→q6, b→q6. At least one pair of states among q0 through q5 is distinguishable by a.
questions.explain: Every a-arrow out of q0 through q5 goes to q1 or q4, and both are final. So a never sends a pair to one final and one non-final state.

questions.q: DFA B over {a, b}: start state q0; every state is final except q6. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q2; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q1, b→q3; q3: a→q4, b→q6; q4: a→q4, b→q5; q5: a→q4, b→q6; q6: a→q6, b→q6. Select every pair that is distinguishable by b.
questions.explain: On b, q3 and q5 go to the non-final q6, while q0, q1, q2 and q4 go to final states. A pair is distinguishable by b exactly when it has one state from {q3, q5} and one from {q0, q1, q2, q4}.

questions.q: DFA B over {a, b}: start state q0; every state is final except q6. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q2; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q1, b→q3; q3: a→q4, b→q6; q4: a→q4, b→q5; q5: a→q4, b→q6; q6: a→q6, b→q6. Which states are combined in the minimized DFA?
choices: q0 with q1, and q3 with q5
q0 with q1, and q2 with q4
q3 with q5 only
q0, q1, q2 and q4 into one state
questions.explain: (q0, q1) go to the same states on both symbols, and so do (q3, q5). The other pairs inside {q0, q1, q2, q4} are all marked using pairs the pre-pass had already marked: (q0,q2), (q1,q2), (q0,q4), (q1,q4) and (q2,q4) all get a 1.

questions.q: DFA B over {a, b}: start state q0; every state is final except q6. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q2; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q1, b→q3; q3: a→q4, b→q6; q4: a→q4, b→q5; q5: a→q4, b→q6; q6: a→q6, b→q6. How many equivalence classes (states of the minimized DFA) are there?
questions.explain: The classes are {q0, q1}, {q2}, {q3, q5}, {q4} and {q6}, so the DFA goes from 7 states to 5.

questions.q: DFA B over {a, b}: start state q0; every state is final except q6. Transitions: q0: a→q1, b→q2; q1: a→q1, b→q2; q2: a→q1, b→q3; q3: a→q4, b→q6; q4: a→q4, b→q5; q5: a→q4, b→q6; q6: a→q6, b→q6. Why can q6 never be combined with another state?
choices: It is the only non-final state
It is unreachable from the start state
It has no outgoing arrows
It is distinguishable from every state by b
questions.explain: Non-final states only combine with non-final states, and q6 is the only one. (q6 is reachable, for example by bbb, and it loops on both symbols. On b it goes to q6, just as q3 does.)

questions.q: In minimized DFA B, the classes are {q0, q1}, {q2}, {q3, q5}, {q4}, {q6}. Originally q3: a→q4, b→q6 and q5: a→q4, b→q6. Where does class {q3, q5} go?
questions.explain: Both members go to q4 on a and to q6 on b. Since they agree, the class is consistent, and its arrows point to the classes containing q4 and q6.

questions.q: How do you draw the arrow on symbol x out of a merged class?
choices: Pick any member q; point to the class holding δ(q, x)
Draw one arrow for each member of the class
Point to the class holding δ(q0, x)
Use only the member with the largest index
questions.explain: "It doesn't have to be all of the states that are in the set, as long as it's one." Every member sends x into the same class, so any member gives the same answer.

questions.q: If two members of a class send symbol a into different classes, there is a mistake in your table.
questions.explain: This is the built-in check. Indistinguishable states always send each symbol into the same class, so a disagreement means those states could not really be combined.

questions.q: A class contains q5 and q6. On b, q6 goes to q5 and q5 goes to q5. What b-arrow does the class get in the minimized DFA?
choices: A b-loop from the class back to itself
A b-arrow to a separate state {q5}
Two b-arrows, one for each member
No b-arrow, since q5 is already in it
questions.explain: q5 is in this same class, so the b-arrow points back to the class itself.

questions.q: Which state is the start state of the minimized DFA?
choices: The class containing q0
The class with the most states
The first final class
The class containing the trap state
questions.explain: The start state is the class that contains the original start state q0.

questions.q: By the course's definition of a DFA, the minimized DFA may leave out the arrows of a trap state (as JFLAP's minimizer sometimes does).
questions.explain: A DFA has an arrow for every symbol out of every state, trap states included. In the 7-state example, {q6} must loop on both a and b.

questions.q: A merged class in the minimized DFA can contain both final and non-final states.
questions.explain: Every final/non-final pair is marked in step 1, so the members of a class always agree. A class is final exactly when its members are final.

questions.q: Why can no DFA accept {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}?
choices: It would need infinitely many states to count a's
It contains the empty string, which DFAs reject
Its strings must alternate between a and b
It is a finite language, too small for a DFA
questions.explain: The machine has to remember how many a's it has read, and that count has no upper bound. A DFA has only finitely many states.

questions.q: How do the regular languages relate to the context-free languages (CFLs)?
choices: Regular languages are a proper subset of CFLs
CFLs are a proper subset of regular languages
The two classes are equal
The two classes are disjoint
questions.explain: Every regular language is context-free, but not the other way around: {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0} is context-free and not regular.

questions.q: Which kind of machine accepts exactly the context-free languages?
choices: Nondeterministic pushdown automata
Deterministic pushdown automata
Nondeterministic finite automata
Deterministic finite automata
questions.explain: NPDAs go with context-free languages the way finite automata go with regular languages. The word "nondeterministic" matters here.

questions.q: What do deterministic pushdown automata accept?
choices: The deterministic CFLs, a proper subset of the CFLs
Exactly the context-free languages
Exactly the regular languages
More languages than nondeterministic PDAs do
questions.explain: Deterministic PDAs define the deterministic context-free languages, a smaller circle inside the CFL circle.

questions.q: DFAs, NFAs and NFA-λs all accept the same class of languages, but deterministic and nondeterministic pushdown automata do not.
questions.explain: Finite automata of all three kinds accept the regular languages (NFA-λ converts to DFA). For PDAs, nondeterminism adds power: NPDAs accept all CFLs, while DPDAs accept only the deterministic CFLs.

questions.q: What does a pushdown automaton add to a finite automaton?
choices: A stack with no size limit
A second input tape
A fixed-size counter
A read-write tape
questions.explain: A PDA is a finite-state automaton plus memory in the form of a stack. The stack has no size limit, so the machine has unbounded memory.

questions.q: Which grammar generates {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}?
choices: S → aSb | λ
S → aS | bS | λ
S → aSa | bSb | λ
S → ab | λ
questions.explain: Each use of S → aSb adds one a on the left and one b on the right, and S → λ ends the derivation. The other grammars generate all strings, even-length palindromes, or only {ab, λ}.

questions.q: How many components does the formal tuple of an NPDA have?
questions.explain: M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, z, F): states, input alphabet, stack alphabet, transition function, initial state, stack start symbol and final states.

questions.q: In M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, z, F), what is z?
choices: A stack symbol that marks the bottom of the stack
An input symbol that marks the end of the input
The state the machine enters when it rejects
The empty string read from the input
questions.explain: z ∈ Γ is the special stack start symbol. Seeing it on top tells the machine its counting symbols are used up.

questions.q: In M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q0, z, F), what is Γ?
choices: The stack alphabet
The input alphabet
The set of final states
The transition function
questions.explain: Σ is the input alphabet and Γ is the stack alphabet. In the lecture's example Σ = {a, b} and Γ = {0, z}.

questions.q: Besides the current state, what determines each move of an NPDA?
choices: The input symbol (or λ) and the top stack symbol
The input symbol and the entire stack contents
The input symbol only
The top stack symbol only
questions.explain: A move reads an input symbol, or nothing in a λ-move, and looks only at the top of the stack. It then replaces that top symbol with a string, which may be λ (a pop).

questions.q: A PDA can still make a move with an empty stack, as long as it has input left to read.
questions.explain: Every move needs a symbol on top of the stack. With an empty stack the machine cannot move at all.

questions.q: δ(q0, a, z) = {(q1, 0z), (q3, λ)}. What does it mean that this set has two elements?
choices: Two separate processes start, one per choice
Only the first pair is used; the second is a backup
Both changes are applied to one stack, in order
The transition is not allowed in an NPDA
questions.explain: This is the nondeterminism. One process goes to q1 and replaces z with 0z, and another goes to q3 and pops z.

questions.q: Stack contents are written as a string with the top on the left. Which symbol is on top of the stack 0z?
questions.explain: The leftmost symbol is the top, so in 0z the 0 is on top and z is at the bottom. This may feel backwards compared with how stacks are drawn in data structures.

questions.q: In a PDA move, replacing the top symbol z with the string 0z has the same effect as pushing a 0.
questions.explain: The z stays at the bottom and a 0 now sits on top of it.

questions.q: In the JFLAP label format "input, pop; push", what does the transition a, 0; 00 do?
choices: Reads a with 0 on top and pushes one more 0
Reads a and pops two 0s off the stack
Reads a only if the stack holds exactly 00
Reads a and replaces the whole stack with 00
questions.explain: The top 0 is replaced by 00, so the net effect is one more 0 on the stack. Only the top symbol is affected.

questions.q: An NPDA for palindromes over {a, b} copies about half of the input onto the stack, then pops while the input matches the top. What is a natural stack alphabet for it?
choices: {a, b, z}
{a, b}
questions.explain: The stack holds copies of the input symbols, plus the special bottom-of-stack symbol z. So the stack alphabet is the input alphabet plus z.

questions.q: NPDA M: states q0–q3, start q0, final state q3, stack alphabet {0, z}, stack starts as z. δ(q0, a, z) = {(q1, 0z), (q3, λ)}; δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}; δ(q1, a, 0) = {(q1, 00)}; δ(q1, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}. Acceptance is by final state. Select every string M accepts.
choices: λ (the empty string)
a
b
ab
aa
aab
aabb
abb
ba
questions.explain: λ is accepted by δ(q0, λ, z), and a by the second choice of δ(q0, a, z). ab and aabb push one 0 per a, pop one 0 per b, then reach q3 when z shows. aa and aab get stuck in q1 or q2 with 0 on top. With abb and b, z is on top while a b is still unread. ba has no b-move from q0.

questions.q: NPDA M: states q0–q3, start q0, final state q3, stack starts as z. δ(q0, a, z) = {(q1, 0z), (q3, λ)}; δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}; δ(q1, a, 0) = {(q1, 00)}; δ(q1, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}. Starting from (q0, aaabbb, z), how many configurations are there after one move?
questions.explain: The two choices of δ(q0, a, z) give (q1, aabbb, 0z) and (q3, aabbb, λ). The λ-move δ(q0, λ, z) gives (q3, aaabbb, λ). Only the q1 process survives.

questions.q: NPDA M: states q0–q3, start q0, final state q3, stack starts as z. δ(q0, a, z) = {(q1, 0z), (q3, λ)}; δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}; δ(q1, a, 0) = {(q1, 00)}; δ(q1, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}. On input aaabbb, why are the two processes that reach q3 on the first move rejected, even though q3 is final?
choices: They still have input to read, with an empty stack
q3 counts as final only for the empty string
They popped z, which a PDA is never allowed to do
They were created by λ-moves, which cannot accept
questions.explain: A process accepts only if it consumes the whole input and ends in a final state. These two processes have input left and an empty stack, so they cannot move and they die.

questions.q: NPDA M: states q0–q3, start q0, final state q3, stack starts as z. δ(q0, a, z) = {(q1, 0z), (q3, λ)}; δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}; δ(q1, a, 0) = {(q1, 00)}; δ(q1, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}. What happens on input aaaa?
choices: Rejected: it ends in q1 with 0 on top and no λ,0 move
Accepted: a process reaches q3 after the first move
Accepted: all four a's are read by the q1 process
Rejected: the stack can hold at most three 0s
questions.explain: The surviving process ends at (q1, λ, 0000z). Every λ-move needs z on top, so it is stuck in q1, which is not final. The q3 processes died with input left. Reading all the input is not enough: the process must also end in a final state.

questions.q: NPDA M: states q0–q3, start q0, final state q3, stack starts as z. δ(q0, a, z) = {(q1, 0z), (q3, λ)}; δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}; δ(q1, a, 0) = {(q1, 00)}; δ(q1, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}. Follow the process that goes through q1 on input aaaabb. After it has read all six symbols, how many 0s are on its stack?
questions.explain: Each a pushes one 0 (z → 0z, then 0 → 00 three times), which gives 0000z. Each b pops one 0, so after two b's the stack is 00z.

questions.q: NPDA M: states q0–q3, start q0, final state q3, stack starts as z. δ(q0, a, z) = {(q1, 0z), (q3, λ)}; δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}; δ(q1, a, 0) = {(q1, 00)}; δ(q1, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}. Why is abb rejected?
choices: After ab, z is on top with b unread; no b-move on z
The stack becomes empty before the first b is read
q2 has no transition that reads b, whatever the top is
It has more a's than b's, so 0s stay on the stack
questions.explain: (q0, abb, z) ⊢ (q1, bb, 0z) ⊢ (q2, b, z). No move reads b with z on top. δ(q2, λ, z) leads to (q3, b, λ), but that process still has input left and an empty stack, so it dies.

questions.category: Acceptance and the language of the example NPDA
questions.q: NPDA M: states q0–q3, start q0, final state q3, stack starts as z. δ(q0, a, z) = {(q1, 0z), (q3, λ)}; δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}; δ(q1, a, 0) = {(q1, 00)}; δ(q1, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}. What is L(M)?
choices: {aⁱbⁱ : i ≥ 0} ∪ {a}
{aⁱbⁱ : i ≥ 0}
{aⁱbⁱ : i ≥ 1} ∪ {a}
{aⁱbʲ : i ≥ j ≥ 0}
questions.explain: The path through q1 and q2 accepts aⁱbⁱ for i ≥ 1, δ(q0, λ, z) accepts λ, and the second choice of δ(q0, a, z) adds the odd extra string a.

questions.category: Acceptance and the language of the example NPDA
questions.q: NPDA M: states q0–q3, start q0, final state q3, stack starts as z. δ(q0, a, z) = {(q1, 0z), (q3, λ)}; δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}; δ(q1, a, 0) = {(q1, 00)}; δ(q1, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}. Which single change makes M accept exactly {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 0}?
choices: Remove the choice (q3, λ) from δ(q0, a, z)
Remove the transition δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}
Make q2 a final state in addition to q3
Remove the transition δ(q2, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}
questions.explain: That choice is the only way to accept the extra string a. Removing δ(q0, λ, z) would lose λ. Removing δ(q2, λ, z) would lose every aⁿbⁿ with n ≥ 1. Making q2 final would accept strings like aab.

questions.category: Acceptance and the language of the example NPDA
questions.q: NPDA M: states q0–q3, start q0, final state q3, stack starts as z. δ(q0, a, z) = {(q1, 0z), (q3, λ)}; δ(q0, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}; δ(q1, a, 0) = {(q1, 00)}; δ(q1, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, b, 0) = {(q2, λ)}; δ(q2, λ, z) = {(q3, λ)}. Which transition lets M accept the empty string?
questions.explain: (q0, λ, z) ⊢ (q3, λ, λ) uses the λ-move out of q0. Nothing is left to read and q3 is final, so λ is accepted.

questions.category: Acceptance and the language of the example NPDA
questions.q: With acceptance by final state, a string is accepted if some process reaches a final state, even with input still unread.
questions.explain: At least one process must consume the whole input and end in a final state.

questions.category: Acceptance and the language of the example NPDA
questions.q: With acceptance by final state, the stack must be empty at the end for the string to be accepted.
questions.explain: The stack contents at the end don't matter ("there may be trash"). That is why changing the last transition to push :) instead of popping made no difference.

questions.category: Acceptance and the language of the example NPDA
questions.q: If a PDA gives the expected answer on every string of length 0 to 6 in a multiple-run test, that proves it accepts the intended language.
questions.explain: Testing on examples is useful, but it is not a proof. A machine can be right on every short string and still be wrong on a longer one.
